name: Aisha Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive for my uncle's haulage firm, six trucks, moving shipping containers from the port to warehouses inland. I collect at the terminal, wait in the queue, get the box on the trailer, and do two or three runs a day. I like the port at dawn, all the cranes and ships. What wears me out is the queuing, sometimes two hours just to get to the crane.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come into the family firm, and how's it going?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle Rafael paid for my licence after I finished school and did a couple of years in his office. I've been driving about a year and a half, and I still get nervous reversing a forty-foot box into the tight bays. I live with my parents, which is normal in our family, and I've saved about four months' worth towards a flat near them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, it's people who run trucks. I'd tell my uncle and the other drivers it's business as usual. Online I'd keep quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle's six trucks are up against companies with six hundred, and that was true long before anyone said AI. The big firms win contracts on price and diesel costs keep going up. So I'm fine for now, but I'm watching the firm's books more than the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and try to get faster at the port so we do one more run a week. I'd help my cousin Nadia in the office chase late payments. I'd keep saving for the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, but a little worried for the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if the firm lost a big contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably park a truck, and as the newest driver, it might be mine. My uncle wouldn't sack me, but I'd be in the office again. That's family, you get moved, not let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you feel about working for family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, sometimes hard. My uncle is strict, but he looks after us. I'd rather work for him than a big firm that doesn't know my name.

I'd tell the drivers it's **business as usual** and keep quiet online.
think: My uncle's **six trucks** compete with firms running hundreds.
I watch the firm's **books** and diesel costs more than robots.
do: Get faster at the port to add **one more run** a week.
Help my cousin chase **late payments** in the office.
Keep saving for a **flat** near my parents.
feel: **Steady**, but a little worried for the firm.

steps.text: Squeeze one more port run into each week
Help Nadia chase late payments in the firm's office
Keep saving for a flat near the family home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small firms need to keep up or they'll go under. I'd tell my uncle we need the new booking tools. I'd probably post less and pray more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the big hauliers let a computer book every container slot at the port, my uncle's firm has to learn it in a year or lose the work. The port's systems will get smarter and faster, and the firms that plug in win. I worry my uncle is too stubborn to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Nadia to show me the port booking software, and I'd use AI now and then to help with emails and quotes. I'd push my uncle, gently, to try one of the planning tools. I'd keep saving and hold off on the flat for a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, for the firm more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it respectfully, at Sunday lunch, not in the office. Something like, we either learn this or the big firms take our port work. He'd grumble but he'd listen if my dad backed me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why hold off on the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the firm shrinks, my wage might drop or I'd go back to the office. I'd rather be living with my parents when that happens than stuck with rent. My mum would be happy anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and families will have to stick together. I'd say the government should help small businesses, not just big ones. At church we'd probably pray about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle built his haulage firm from one second-hand truck, and I'd hate to be the generation that watches it sold for scrap. The thinking AI takes the office and bookings in 2028. Then the port's robot trucks come around 2031, and our six drivers are done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop saving for the flat and put my money into the family pot. I'd learn the AI tools properly to help run the firm's office cheaper. And I'd look at a job that's about people, maybe care work, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the family's ground is shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for the firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we might survive 2028 by using the cheap AI for our bookings. But by 2031 the port will want robot trucks, and we can't afford those. So three years of struggling, then probably selling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My parents, my uncle, our church. In our family, nobody gets laid off; they just get moved to the office or the kitchen. But if the firm's gone, there's nowhere to move to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people are sensible. I'd say small firms need help and time. I'd say it calmly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for my cousin and me to drag my uncle's firm into the computer age, if he lets us. Robots around 2034 is a while off. I think we'd have a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the booking and planning software properly this year. I'd help Nadia move the firm onto AI scheduling so we compete on price. I'd still save for the flat, a bit slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your uncle refuses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd wait a year and ask again. He's stubborn but not stupid. If he still refused, I'd quietly look for a job at a bigger firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would leaving the family firm mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would feel like a betrayal, honestly. My mum would understand, my uncle maybe not. I'd only do it if I really had to.

say: I'd say five years is enough if people are **sensible**.
I'd calmly say small firms need **help and time**.
think: My cousin and I could drag the firm into the **computer age**.
Robots around **2034** give us a real chance.
do: Learn **booking and planning** software this year.

Keep saving for the flat, **more slowly**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough for my cousin and me to drag my uncle's firm into the computer age, if he lets us.
fieldNote: Aisha sees herself and her cousin as the firm's **modernisers**.

steps.text: Move the firm's scheduling onto AI software with Nadia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and small firms can adapt. I'd tell other family firms to start planning. I'd say it at church too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years, I'd want the family firm to be the one the port trusts to run the robot trucks safely. Robots around 2039 means I'd be 40. I'd hope by then I'd be helping run the firm, not driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive and learn the office side over a few years. Around 2034 I'd look at whether the firm can lease a robot truck to trial. I'd buy the flat near my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Hopeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think a six-truck firm could really run robot trucks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not alone. We might team up with two other family firms. My uncle knows them from the port.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your life look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Married, I hope, with a flat near my parents. Running the office with Nadia. Not rich, but steady.

fieldNote: Aisha imagines the firm **adapting** rather than dying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the family firm wouldn't have time to adapt. What would help is support for small firms, like loans to buy new trucks or software, and training for family businesses. In my family, nobody gets laid off; they just get moved to the office or the kitchen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about faith and family. People like us lean on each other first. That's the real safety net.

headlineQuote: In my family, nobody gets laid off; they just get moved to the office or the kitchen.
portrait: Aisha Reyes, 27, drives **port containers** for her uncle's six-truck haulage firm.
Her worry is the **family firm**, squeezed by big rivals even without AI.
In the fast picture she fears the firm is **sold**, and puts savings into the family pot.
With more time she imagines **modernising** the firm with her cousin Nadia.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as the family firm would have no time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: **Loans and training** for small family firms to buy trucks or software.
